plans.label: Lesson 01
plans.title: Observe and describe
plans.objective: Record two observations of a classroom object and identify the sense or tool used.
plans.materials: Leaf, hand lens, observation slip

phases.teacher: Show a leaf and ask for one feature another pupil could check.
phases.pupils: Inspect the leaf and name a visible feature.

phases.teacher: Model recording colour and texture with a sense or hand lens, then hand out two leaves.
phases.pupils: Examine one leaf, record two observations and name the sense or tool used for each.

phases.teacher: Check that each statement describes a property visible or detectable on the leaf.
phases.pupils: Individually record two observations with their sense or tool.

phases.teacher: Ask how a partner could check an observation about the edge.
phases.pupils: Point to the edge and describe what to look for.

plans.follow_up: Practise turning opinions about an object into checkable observations.

plans.label: Lesson 02
plans.title: Classify by a shared feature
plans.objective: Sort a set of leaves into two groups and state the rule used.
plans.materials: Six fallen leaves, sorting mats, exit slips

phases.teacher: Show two leaves with different edges and ask how they differ.
phases.pupils: Describe each edge using a visible characteristic.

phases.teacher: Model a two-group sort by smooth or toothed edge. Give six leaves with clear edges.
phases.pupils: Agree a rule, place each leaf once and compare the groups.

phases.teacher: Check an individual sort of the same six leaves and the written rule.
phases.pupils: Sort all six independently and write the rule.

phases.teacher: Show an unfamiliar leaf with a toothed edge.
phases.pupils: Place it in the toothed group and name the evidence.

plans.follow_up: Re-sort a set using one feature consistently.

plans.label: Lesson 03
plans.title: Measure using standard units
plans.objective: Measure three objects with a ruler and record each result in centimetres.
plans.materials: Rulers marked in centimetres, eraser, pencil, card strip

phases.teacher: Place a strip at the 1 cm mark and ask where it should begin.
phases.pupils: Point to zero and explain the alignment.

phases.teacher: Demonstrate reading a ruler from above. Set out objects shorter than each ruler.
phases.pupils: Measure the eraser, pencil and strip from zero and record each length.

phases.teacher: Observe one check measurement per pupil and verify all three readings and units.
phases.pupils: Submit three lengths in cm and demonstrate one reading.

phases.teacher: Show a ruler with a gap before zero.
phases.pupils: Explain why the scale start and ruler edge differ.

plans.follow_up: Repeat one reading with the object correctly aligned.

plans.label: Lesson 04
plans.title: Infer and predict
plans.objective: Separate an observation from its inference and justify a prediction using the available evidence.
plans.materials: Before-and-after puddle pictures with times, comparison cards

phases.teacher: Show a large puddle at 9 a.m. and a smaller one at 10 a.m.
phases.pupils: State one visible change.

phases.teacher: Separate a recorded detail from an inference. Compare equal cups of water kept in shade and sun using picture data.
phases.pupils: Mark the difference, infer why it occurred and predict which level will fall more by noon.

phases.teacher: Check three labelled responses and a prediction that cites the trend shown.
phases.pupils: Write an observation, an inference and an evidence-based prediction.

phases.teacher: Ask which statement could be checked at noon.
phases.pupils: Identify the prediction and say what to measure.

plans.follow_up: Give another example of a recorded fact and a possible explanation.

plans.label: Lesson 05
plans.title: Present observations in time order
plans.objective: Sequence the changes in an observation and communicate the sequence in a labelled table.
plans.materials: Four timestamped pictures of an ice cube melting, table slips

phases.teacher: Show the first and last images with times covered.
phases.pupils: Suggest which came earlier and give one clue.

phases.teacher: Reveal times and model a table with time and visible change as headings.
phases.pupils: Order all four pictures and enter one observable change for each time.

phases.teacher: Check sequence and headings on each pupil's own table.
phases.pupils: Submit a labelled time table covering all four pictures.

phases.teacher: Show a mixed-up pair of images.
phases.pupils: Correct their order using a timestamp and a visible clue.

plans.follow_up: Practise matching time labels to changes in a new sequence.

plans.label: Lesson 06
plans.title: Interpret an observed trend
plans.objective: Use two values from a results table to explain how the measured outcome changes.
plans.materials: Plant height table, rulers, slips

phases.teacher: Display heights of 4 cm and 7 cm taken a week apart.
phases.pupils: State which measurement is greater and by how much.

phases.teacher: Use a table for four weeks showing 4, 7, 9 and 11 cm. Model a trend statement supported by two readings.
phases.pupils: Compare pairs of readings and explain the overall change to a partner.

phases.teacher: Check a trend statement with two values and their units.
phases.pupils: Individually cite weeks 1 and 4 and explain the 7 cm increase.

phases.teacher: Ask if every interval had the same increase.
phases.pupils: Compare 3 cm between weeks 1 and 2 with 2 cm between weeks 2 and 3.

plans.follow_up: Ask pupils to cite exact evidence before stating a trend.

plans.label: Lesson 07
plans.title: Define an outcome operationally
plans.objective: Write an observable test for a property and use it consistently on two examples.
plans.materials: Paper towel, waxed paper, equal drops of water, timer

phases.teacher: Show water beading on waxed paper.
phases.pupils: Suggest a visible test for whether a material absorbs water.

phases.teacher: Agree an operational rule. Place one drop on each material and check for a surface droplet after ten seconds.
phases.pupils: Apply the same rule and time to paper towel and waxed paper, then record results.

phases.teacher: Check whether pupils define the procedure and record both visible outcomes.
phases.pupils: Individually describe the agreed test and classify both samples from their observations.

phases.teacher: Ask why the wait time must stay fixed.
phases.pupils: Explain how changing the time could change the result.

plans.follow_up: Ask pupils to replace broad descriptors with observable criteria.

plans.label: Lesson 08
plans.title: Choose variables and test a prediction
plans.objective: Identify the three variable types and write a testable hypothesis linking two of them.
plans.materials: Card, toy car, ramp supports, measuring tape, planning sheet

phases.teacher: Raise one end of a toy-car ramp and ask what changes.
phases.pupils: Name ramp height and suggest a result to measure.

phases.teacher: Keep one car and track. Model a statement linking ramp height and travel distance, then show a pair of proposed trials.
phases.pupils: Name the height, distance and two controls. Write a prediction that can be checked in class.

phases.teacher: Use a planning slip to check all three variable types and a hypothesis linking height and distance.
phases.pupils: Submit one named variable of each type and a testable hypothesis.

phases.teacher: Ask if swapping the car would test ramp height fairly.
phases.pupils: Identify the problem and name the control.

plans.follow_up: Rewrite the hypothesis using a variable that can be measured.

plans.label: Lesson 09
plans.title: Plan a fair investigation
plans.objective: Write the aim, materials, steps and results-table headings for a fair test.
plans.materials: Toy car, ramp, blocks, tape measure, experiment planner

phases.teacher: Show two ramp runs that use different cars and heights.
phases.pupils: Identify why the results cannot isolate height.

phases.teacher: Show available equipment. Model marking the same release line and measuring from the ramp end.
phases.pupils: Plan two ramp heights with three repeats per height, a fixed release point and a results table.

phases.teacher: Check each plan includes an aim, equipment, steps and headings with a distance unit.
phases.pupils: Submit an individual plan that changes only ramp height and records travel distance.

phases.teacher: Ask where measurements begin if the car rolls beyond the ramp.
phases.pupils: Point to the fixed ramp-end mark and explain its use.

plans.follow_up: Flag a missing control or unclear measurement start before Lesson 10.

plans.label: Lesson 10
plans.title: Collect data and report a conclusion
plans.objective: Carry out the planned investigation and compare the measured results with the hypothesis in a short report.
plans.materials: Lesson 09 planner, ramp, toy car, blocks, tape, report slip

phases.teacher: Ask the class to recall its hypothesis and measurement start.
phases.pupils: Restate the hypothesis and point to the ramp-end mark.

phases.teacher: Supervise three runs at each height. Remind groups to release without pushing and keep the path clear.
phases.pupils: Run the trial, measure six distances and look for a repeated pattern.

phases.teacher: Check the table and a conclusion that cites results and addresses the hypothesis.
phases.pupils: Submit a short report with results for both heights and a data-supported conclusion.

phases.teacher: Ask how to handle a run in which the car veered off track.
phases.pupils: Describe the problem, record it and repeat the run with the same controls.

plans.follow_up: Repeat a trial or revise the conclusion when the evidence is mixed.

plans.label: Review 01
plans.title: Scientific Skills Review
plans.objective: Use a results table to identify the variables, state a trend and rewrite a conclusion.
plans.materials: Ramp results table, conclusion cards

phases.teacher: Show two distances and ask what was changed.
phases.pupils: Identify the trial condition from the headings.

phases.teacher: Provide a table comparing two ramp heights and three runs each.
phases.pupils: Mark the variable and say whether the results show a consistent trend.

phases.teacher: Check a conclusion rewritten to include one measured comparison.
phases.pupils: Individually identify a variable, state the trend and rewrite the conclusion using two values.

phases.teacher: Ask how many variables should change in one fair comparison.
phases.pupils: Name one change and one control.

plans.follow_up: Revisit any science process skill not shown independently.

plans.label: Lesson 11
plans.title: Trace the path of air
plans.objective: Label the nose, trachea and lungs, then trace air during inhalation and exhalation.
plans.materials: Airway diagram, organ labels, arrow strips

phases.teacher: Ask pupils where air goes after it enters the nose.
phases.pupils: Point towards the lungs on a silhouette.

phases.teacher: Trace the route on a diagram and reverse the arrows for exhalation.
phases.pupils: Label nose, trachea and lungs, then trace both directions to a partner.

phases.teacher: Check three correctly placed labels and both arrow routes on a fresh diagram.
phases.pupils: Complete and label both routes independently.

phases.teacher: Ask which tube carries air between the nose and lungs.
phases.pupils: Name the trachea and point to it.

plans.follow_up: Repeat tracing using arrows of two colours.

plans.label: Lesson 12
plans.title: Compare inhaled and exhaled air
plans.objective: Compare oxygen and carbon dioxide in the two air samples using a two-column diagram.
plans.materials: Textbook air-composition diagrams, oxygen and carbon dioxide labels

phases.teacher: Show the two air-sample headings and ask what they mean.
phases.pupils: Identify air entering and leaving the body.

phases.teacher: Use the textbook diagrams to compare the two gases. Give arrows to represent more or less of each gas.
phases.pupils: Construct a two-column comparison and explain the direction of change for each gas.

phases.teacher: Check both changes and whether pupils recognise both gases in both samples.
phases.pupils: Label the two columns and compare oxygen and carbon dioxide independently.

phases.teacher: Ask if exhaled air still contains oxygen.
phases.pupils: Use the comparison to answer yes and explain.

plans.follow_up: Practise describing relative amounts using the diagrams.

plans.label: Lesson 13
plans.title: Observe chest movement
plans.objective: Use a diagram to explain what happens to the chest during inhalation and exhalation.
plans.materials: Chest diagrams, arrow stickers, observation slips

phases.teacher: Ask pupils to place hands lightly on their own ribs and breathe normally.
phases.pupils: Notice whether the chest moves outwards or inwards.

phases.teacher: Show paired chest diagrams. Model arrows for chest movement during a calm breath.
phases.pupils: Observe a normal breath and mark outward and inward movement on the two diagrams.

phases.teacher: Check pupils explain both directions of chest movement.
phases.pupils: Individually label inhalation and exhalation and explain the movement in each.

phases.teacher: Show an outward arrow without a label.
phases.pupils: Identify inhalation and explain the clue.

plans.follow_up: Pair each chest movement with the correct air-flow arrow.

plans.label: Lesson 14
plans.title: Compare breathing rates
plans.objective: Count breaths at rest and after light movement, then use the results to explain the difference.
plans.materials: Timer, breathing-count table, light-movement alternative dataset

phases.teacher: Ask what one breath means for counting.
phases.pupils: Describe one complete inhalation and exhalation.

phases.teacher: Time a resting count and another after 30 seconds of gentle marching. Provide sample data to pupils who sit out.
phases.pupils: Record counts for equal time intervals and compare the two results.

phases.teacher: Check a comparison using two numbers and an explanation connected to activity.
phases.pupils: Write both counts and explain the difference using the recorded evidence.

phases.teacher: Ask why the same count duration matters.
phases.pupils: Explain how different count durations affect comparison.

plans.follow_up: Use a worked example to connect equal counting time with a fair comparison.

plans.label: Lesson 15
plans.title: Excretion and defecation
plans.objective: Match organs to excretory products and explain the difference between excretion and defecation.
plans.materials: Cards for lungs, skin, kidneys and intestines; product cards

phases.teacher: Show a sweat droplet icon and a faeces icon.
phases.pupils: Name two things the body removes.

phases.teacher: Model the distinction between removing waste made by the body and removing undigested food.
phases.pupils: Match lungs to carbon dioxide and water vapour, kidneys to urine, and skin to sweat. Place faeces under defecation.

phases.teacher: Check the organ-product matches and the written distinction between the two processes.
phases.pupils: Submit matches and explain the distinction in one sentence.

phases.teacher: Ask whether faeces is an example of excretion.
phases.pupils: Identify defecation and explain using undigested food.

plans.follow_up: Revisit the origin of each waste product with the organ cards.

plans.label: Lesson 16
plans.title: Why the body removes waste
plans.objective: Use a body diagram and one example to explain why removal of waste matters.
plans.materials: Body outline, urine and faeces route cards, response slips

phases.teacher: Ask what happens to waste after the body produces it.
phases.pupils: Suggest why waste needs a way out.

phases.teacher: Trace urine formation and removal using a simple diagram, then contrast the route of undigested food.
phases.pupils: Label the exit routes and discuss why the two removal processes are needed.

phases.teacher: Check each pupil's diagram and one supported explanation of why removal matters.
phases.pupils: Annotate a route and explain why the body must remove the material.

phases.teacher: Ask pupils to name the two processes from the diagrams.
phases.pupils: Identify each process from the material being removed.

plans.follow_up: Review waste routes separately with pupils who conflate them.

plans.label: Lesson 17
plans.title: Identify a stimulus and response
plans.objective: Match three stimuli to their sensory organs and the corresponding responses.
plans.materials: Scenario cards, stimulus–organ–response table

phases.teacher: Tap a desk softly and ask what caused a pupil to look.
phases.pupils: Name the sound and the response.

phases.teacher: Model the table with sound, ear and turning the head. Provide light, sound and touch scenarios.
phases.pupils: Complete three scenarios and trace each link aloud with a partner.

phases.teacher: Check all three chains for a plausible organ and response.
phases.pupils: Submit three complete stimulus–organ–response matches.

phases.teacher: Show a cool object touching skin in a picture.
phases.pupils: Identify the skin and describe a plausible response.

plans.follow_up: Practise distinguishing an external stimulus from the action it causes.

plans.label: Lesson 18
plans.title: Explain how responses protect people
plans.objective: Explain a protective response and show how one habit can interfere with it.
plans.materials: Protective response and distraction scenario cards, exit slips

phases.teacher: Show a picture of a pupil blinking when dust approaches.
phases.pupils: Describe what the blink protects.

phases.teacher: Compare blinking with turning towards a warning sound. Discuss how loud headphones can mask a warning sound.
phases.pupils: Draw a stimulus-to-response chain and explain the protective effect, then annotate how the habit interferes.

phases.teacher: Check a protective example and a separate explanation of the effect of the habit.
phases.pupils: Submit both explanations with the stimulus and response identified.

phases.teacher: Ask pupils to recommend one safer habit near traffic.
phases.pupils: Explain how making warning sounds easier to hear helps.

plans.follow_up: Revisit a scenario where the habit changes detection of the stimulus.

plans.label: Review 02
plans.title: Humans Review
plans.objective: Label the breathing organs, then link one sensory response and one waste-removal process to their functions.
plans.materials: Blank airway chart, response and waste cards

phases.teacher: Show one unlabeled airway picture.
phases.pupils: Identify one organ based on its location.

phases.teacher: Set three short tasks covering air flow, sensory response and waste removal.
phases.pupils: Complete all three tasks, then check labels against the textbook.

phases.teacher: Check each pupil's airway labels and functional explanation for one response and one waste process.
phases.pupils: Submit the completed review slip independently.

phases.teacher: Ask how recognising a stimulus can protect the body.
phases.pupils: Give one example and explain the protection.

plans.follow_up: Use review slips to identify which of the three ideas needs practice.

plans.label: Lesson 19
plans.title: Sort animals by breathing organ
plans.objective: Label four breathing organs and classify example animals by the organ used.
plans.materials: Pictures of fish, adult mammals, insects and earthworms; organ labels

phases.teacher: Display a fish and ask which organ takes oxygen from water.
phases.pupils: Identify the gills.

phases.teacher: Model a sort for gills, lungs, breathing tubes and moist skin. Give two example cards per group.
phases.pupils: Sort examples and match each breathing organ to its diagram.

phases.teacher: Check four organ labels and one accurate animal match for each.
phases.pupils: Label and classify one example for each of the four organs.

phases.teacher: Ask where an earthworm belongs and why.
phases.pupils: Name moist skin and explain the visible grouping rule.

plans.follow_up: Pair unfamiliar animals with textbook diagrams to check the organ.

plans.label: Lesson 20
plans.title: Breathing in water and on land
plans.objective: Compare a frog with another animal and explain the role of each organ in its habitat.
plans.materials: Adult frog and fish diagrams, habitat cards

phases.teacher: Show a frog partly submerged at a pond edge.
phases.pupils: Suggest where the animal can obtain oxygen.

phases.teacher: Compare the adult frog's lungs and moist skin with a fish's gills. Distinguish adult frogs from tadpoles if asked.
phases.pupils: Match the adult frog's breathing routes to land or water, then compare with the fish.

phases.teacher: Check a two-animal comparison with an explanation of the organs in each setting.
phases.pupils: Write how the adult frog can breathe on land and in water and how the fish differs.

phases.teacher: Ask why a fish cannot use a frog's lungs.
phases.pupils: Point to the different organs and state how each is used.

plans.follow_up: Practise labeling the adult life stage in an animal comparison.

plans.label: Lesson 21
plans.title: Vertebrates and invertebrates
plans.objective: Classify unfamiliar animals by presence of a backbone and justify two choices.
plans.materials: Animal picture cards, diagram cards showing internal structures

phases.teacher: Show an animal silhouette and ask what hidden clue might help classify it.
phases.pupils: Suggest looking for a backbone.

phases.teacher: Model the backbone rule using a fish skeleton and a snail picture. Give unfamiliar examples with structure cards.
phases.pupils: Group the examples and link each choice to the evidence supplied.

phases.teacher: Check all four individual placements and justification for two.
phases.pupils: Individually sort four examples and explain two using the backbone rule.

phases.teacher: Ask whether a hard shell is evidence of a backbone.
phases.pupils: Use the snail example to explain the difference.

plans.follow_up: Revisit internal structure instead of external covering when sorting.

plans.label: Lesson 22
plans.title: Compare vertebrate groups
plans.objective: Use body coverings, breathing organs and reproduction to identify examples from the five vertebrate groups.
plans.materials: Vertebrate group cards, example and feature cards

phases.teacher: Compare a bird and a fish with pictures.
phases.pupils: Name one observable difference.

phases.teacher: Build a five-group chart using selected examples and features of fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
phases.pupils: Use body covering, breathing and reproduction clues to classify the given examples.

phases.teacher: Check five individual group matches and an evidence-based explanation for two.
phases.pupils: Classify five examples and cite a feature for two choices.

phases.teacher: Ask why a whale remains a mammal though it lives in water.
phases.pupils: Cite breathing lungs and feeding young with milk.

plans.follow_up: Give one example for a group that was confused on the exit slip.

plans.label: Review 03
plans.title: Animals Review
plans.objective: Identify a vertebrate group from its characteristics and explain the breathing organs of two animals.
plans.materials: Three animal cards, feature chart, individual slip

phases.teacher: Show a feather and ask which vertebrate group it suggests.
phases.pupils: Name birds and cite the feather.

phases.teacher: Provide one unfamiliar vertebrate clue set and two animal breathing examples.
phases.pupils: Identify a group, then match both animals to their breathing organs.

phases.teacher: Check group reasoning and the two organ explanations.
phases.pupils: Submit an independently labelled review slip.

phases.teacher: Ask how breathing and backbone grouping differ.
phases.pupils: Give one example showing the distinction.

plans.follow_up: Target the classification or breathing clue that needs revision.

plans.label: Lesson 23
plans.title: Match plant parts to stimuli
plans.objective: Match roots, shoots or leaves to a stimulus and predict the direction or type of response.
plans.materials: Photos of seedlings and Mimosa, stimulus labels

phases.teacher: Show Mimosa leaves before and after touch.
phases.pupils: Describe the change without guessing the cause.

phases.teacher: Compare images or clips for light, gravity, moisture and touch. Model linking one plant part to one stimulus.
phases.pupils: Match roots, shoots and leaves to cards and predict the response for each pictured setup.

phases.teacher: Check matches and one predicted direction or movement with a reason.
phases.pupils: Individually label three examples and explain one predicted change.

phases.teacher: Ask which part grows towards a light opening in a box.
phases.pupils: Name the shoot and indicate the direction of growth.

plans.follow_up: Use new diagrams to distinguish plant part, stimulus and response.

plans.label: Lesson 24
plans.title: Investigate a plant response
plans.objective: Set up a comparison for one stimulus and record the initial position and conditions.
plans.materials: Two similar seedlings, two boxes, watering measure, dated observation cards

phases.teacher: Show two boxes, one with side light and one with overhead light.
phases.pupils: Predict how the direction of light may affect the shoots.

phases.teacher: Set up matched seedlings and agree constant watering and observation times. Mark initial shoot directions.
phases.pupils: Prepare both setups, label the light direction and draw the starting shoots.

phases.teacher: Check individual diagrams and labels for the variable and initial conditions.
phases.pupils: Submit a dated diagram for both seedlings and a prediction.

phases.teacher: Agree when the class will next look at the plants.
phases.pupils: Record one recurring observation time.

plans.follow_up: Use class observations between Lessons 24 and 26. Keep teacher-prepared examples for comparison.

plans.label: Lesson 25
plans.title: Inputs and products of photosynthesis
plans.objective: Label a flow diagram showing what a plant needs to make food and what the process produces.
plans.materials: Photosynthesis input/output labels, arrows, leaf diagram

phases.teacher: Ask where the material for a plant's food comes from.
phases.pupils: Offer possible inputs for the class to sort.

phases.teacher: Model sunlight as the energy source, chlorophyll as the pigment and water and carbon dioxide as inputs. Trace sugar and oxygen as products.
phases.pupils: Build and explain an input–process–output diagram with cards.

phases.teacher: Check whether each pupil assigns all labels and defines photosynthesis in simple language.
phases.pupils: Complete the diagram independently and state that plants make their own food.

phases.teacher: Point to chlorophyll and ask where it is found.
phases.pupils: Identify the green leaf as the location in this model.

plans.follow_up: Re-sort requirements and products with pupils who mix the two sides.

plans.label: Lesson 26
plans.title: Explain the plant investigation
plans.objective: Use dated observations from the two setups to draw a conclusion about the chosen stimulus.
plans.materials: Lesson 24 drawings, dated seedling observations, photos

phases.teacher: Compare the starting and latest shoot pictures without labels.
phases.pupils: Describe one change in the shoot direction.

phases.teacher: Lay out the dated records for both conditions. Ask groups what stayed the same and which evidence supports the result.
phases.pupils: Order the records and compare the growth direction of the paired seedlings.

phases.teacher: Check a conclusion using two dated observations, including both setups.
phases.pupils: Write a conclusion about shoot growth towards light and cite the recorded comparison.

phases.teacher: Ask why a single photograph gives weaker evidence.
phases.pupils: Explain why the starting conditions and another setup support the conclusion.

plans.follow_up: Provide the dated class example to any group with incomplete observations.

plans.label: Lesson 27
plans.title: Photosynthesis and living things
plans.objective: Use a food-and-oxygen diagram to explain two ways living things depend on photosynthesis.
plans.materials: Food-chain cards, oxygen arrows, plant-to-animal diagram

phases.teacher: Show a grass–rabbit relationship and ask where the rabbit gets food.
phases.pupils: Identify the plant as the source.

phases.teacher: Model how plant-produced food supports feeding relationships and how oxygen produced by plants supports breathing.
phases.pupils: Use arrows to explain a local plant–animal food link and the role of oxygen.

phases.teacher: Check both dependency explanations with correctly directed arrows.
phases.pupils: Submit an annotated diagram explaining one food link and one oxygen link.

phases.teacher: Ask pupils how a plant can support an animal that does not eat plants.
phases.pupils: Trace an indirect food link through a plant-eating animal.

plans.follow_up: Revisit the arrows in one three-organism chain.

plans.label: Review 04
plans.title: Plants Review
plans.objective: Link two plant stimuli to responses and explain which inputs a plant needs for photosynthesis.
plans.materials: Four plant pictures, blank photosynthesis diagram, review slips

phases.teacher: Show a paired image of a shoot bending and a Mimosa leaf closing.
phases.pupils: Name one stimulus for each picture.

phases.teacher: Set two response questions and one photosynthesis diagram task.
phases.pupils: Match the stimuli and plant responses and place the diagram labels.

phases.teacher: Check two correct stimulus links and the photosynthesis inputs.
phases.pupils: Submit both matches and state the role of sunlight in the diagram.

phases.teacher: Ask which labels identify products.
phases.pupils: Name sugar and oxygen.

plans.follow_up: Review stimuli and photosynthesis separately where answers overlap.

plans.label: Lesson 28
plans.title: Trace a straight path of light
plans.objective: Align holes in three cards and use the observation to explain why a light spot disappears when one card moves.
plans.materials: Three holed cards, stands, LED torch, white screen

phases.teacher: Show a spot on the screen and cover one card hole.
phases.pupils: Predict what will happen when the hole is covered.

phases.teacher: Align the three holes and use an LED torch facing the screen. Move the middle card sideways for a comparison.
phases.pupils: Observe and record the aligned and moved results. Sketch the path with arrows.

phases.teacher: Check two observations and an explanation linking the loss of the spot to the straight path.
phases.pupils: Sketch both setups and explain why the spot disappears.

phases.teacher: Ask how to make the spot return.
phases.pupils: Realign the card with the other holes.

plans.follow_up: Repeat the comparison with the torch aimed only at the screen.

plans.label: Lesson 29
plans.title: Compare the clarity of shadows
plans.objective: Test three materials under the same light and classify them using the shadows observed.
plans.materials: Clear plastic, tracing paper, card, LED torch and screen

phases.teacher: Hold three samples up and ask which allows the most light through.
phases.pupils: Make a prediction for the three samples.

phases.teacher: Fix lamp, sample and screen positions. Test each sample in the same frame.
phases.pupils: Compare the clarity and darkness of the shadows and record the light transmitted.

phases.teacher: Check three classifications using observed shadow differences.
phases.pupils: Individually classify the samples as transparent, translucent or opaque with evidence.

phases.teacher: Ask why tracing paper makes a different shadow from clear plastic.
phases.pupils: Refer to light passing through and scattering in the tracing paper.

plans.follow_up: Repeat one comparison using equal source and screen distances.

plans.label: Lesson 30
plans.title: Investigate shadow size
plans.objective: Change one distance and record how the shadow size changes while keeping the other distance fixed.
plans.materials: Torch, opaque shape, screen, ruler, distance marks

phases.teacher: Show two shadows of one object and ask how the sizes can differ.
phases.pupils: Suggest a change in position while keeping the object unchanged.

phases.teacher: Fix the object and screen and mark two torch positions. For a second comparison, fix the torch and object and mark two screen positions.
phases.pupils: Keep the object facing the same way. Test two positions in each comparison and record the distances and shadow widths in cm.

phases.teacher: Check two comparisons and the distance held fixed in each. Use the observed readings as the answer key.
phases.pupils: Use two readings to explain which torch position made the larger shadow. Use the second comparison to explain the effect of moving the screen.

phases.teacher: Ask what to keep fixed in a repeat trial.
phases.pupils: Name the object and screen positions or object orientation.

plans.follow_up: Use a setup sketch to distinguish the distance changed from the distance kept fixed.

plans.label: Lesson 31
plans.title: Investigate shadow shape
plans.objective: Alter the position or orientation of an object and explain the resulting shadow using labelled sketches.
plans.materials: Opaque rectangular card, torch, fixed stand, screen, tracing paper

phases.teacher: Hold a card face-on and edge-on without changing its centre position.
phases.pupils: Predict how the shadow outline changes.

phases.teacher: Fix the torch and screen while rotating the card. Then fix the card and screen and compare a torch in front with a torch off to one side.
phases.pupils: Trace and label two outlines for each comparison. Mark the orientation of the card or the position of the torch on each sketch.

phases.teacher: Check a pair of labelled outlines and ask pupils to trace a straight path from the torch past an edge of the card to the screen.
phases.pupils: Compare the two outlines in one pair. Explain how changing the card orientation or torch position changes where the card blocks the light.

phases.teacher: Ask whether replacing the object would answer the same question.
phases.pupils: Explain why the same object should be used to test orientation.

plans.follow_up: Repeat with another object only after explaining the first comparison.

plans.label: Lesson 32
plans.title: Reflect light with a mirror
plans.objective: Redirect a beam with a mirror and identify a daily use of the same property.
plans.materials: Flat acrylic mirror, torch, white screen, road-mirror pictures

phases.teacher: Show a mirror near a white screen and ask how to move the light spot.
phases.pupils: Suggest changing the mirror's angle.

phases.teacher: Aim the torch away from faces, towards the mirror. Rotate the mirror to redirect the beam to two marks.
phases.pupils: Observe the change in spot position and match the principle to a road mirror or periscope picture.

phases.teacher: Check one observed redirection and one daily use with an explanation.
phases.pupils: Draw the torch, mirror and screen and identify a use of reflected light.

phases.teacher: Ask what the mirror changes in the setup.
phases.pupils: State that it changes the direction of the light.

plans.follow_up: Practise linking the use to the reflected path shown in the diagram.

plans.label: Lesson 33
plans.title: Draw a reflected light path
plans.objective: Draw a ray diagram with arrows and use it to explain where light travels after striking a mirror.
plans.materials: Mirror, ray-path tracing sheet, rulers, pencils

phases.teacher: Show two rays drawn without arrowheads.
phases.pupils: Identify which ray should point towards the mirror.

phases.teacher: Use the mirror setup and trace source-to-mirror and mirror-to-screen segments. Place arrows on both segments.
phases.pupils: Mark where light reaches the mirror, then draw and explain both paths.

phases.teacher: Check a labelled diagram with two directional arrows and a correct explanation.
phases.pupils: Independently draw a different mirror placement using a supplied reflected spot.

phases.teacher: Ask where a light ray begins on each diagram.
phases.pupils: Point to the source and follow the arrow directions.

plans.follow_up: Recheck arrow directions before adding labels.

plans.label: Lesson 34
plans.title: Observe refraction in water
plans.objective: Sketch how a pencil or coin appears through water and identify a second example of refraction.
plans.materials: Clear cup, water, pencil, printed coin example

phases.teacher: Show a pencil in an empty cup from the side.
phases.pupils: Sketch its straight appearance.

phases.teacher: Add water and keep the viewing position fixed. Show the coin example as a separate case.
phases.pupils: Compare and sketch the pencil in air and water, then identify refraction in the coin example.

phases.teacher: Check an annotated before-and-after sketch and the second example.
phases.pupils: Submit a sketch and explain that light changes direction at the boundary.

phases.teacher: Ask whether the pencil itself changed shape.
phases.pupils: Use the original object and viewing evidence to explain.

plans.follow_up: Revisit the boundary where the light changes direction.

plans.label: Lesson 35
plans.title: Explain rainbow formation
plans.objective: Record the colours observed when white light passes through water and relate the result to a rainbow.
plans.materials: White light source, water tray and acrylic mirror, white card, rainbow photo

phases.teacher: Show a rainbow photo and ask why many colours appear.
phases.pupils: Suggest a link to sunlight and raindrops.

phases.teacher: Use a teacher-led white-light demonstration with water, acrylic mirror and white card. Supply an observed result photo if lighting prevents a clear display.
phases.pupils: Record visible colours and connect the water demonstration to light interacting with raindrops.

phases.teacher: Check a colour record and an explanation linking white light and water to the rainbow.
phases.pupils: Individually explain the connection using an annotated diagram.

phases.teacher: Ask where the colours begin in the demonstration.
phases.pupils: Identify white light as the source and water as part of the setup.

plans.follow_up: Use a recorded photo to check the observation under better lighting.

plans.label: Review 05
plans.title: Properties of Light Review
plans.objective: Explain a shadow change and use a ray diagram to distinguish reflection from refraction.
plans.materials: Shadow sketches, mirror diagram, pencil-in-water image

phases.teacher: Show two shadow drawings with different widths.
phases.pupils: Name one position change that could explain the difference.

phases.teacher: Give one shadow comparison, one mirror diagram and one water-boundary diagram.
phases.pupils: Annotate the three examples using labels for the behaviours of light.

phases.teacher: Check the shadow explanation and two distinct ray sketches.
phases.pupils: Submit an explanation of the shadow change and distinguish reflection from refraction.

phases.teacher: Ask which case involves light changing direction at a boundary into water.
phases.pupils: Identify the refraction example.

plans.follow_up: Assign the diagram with the least secure explanation for follow-up.

plans.label: Lesson 36
plans.title: Vibrations and sound direction
plans.objective: Show a vibrating source and use observations from different positions to describe how sound travels.
plans.materials: Rubber bands on boxes, rice on a membrane, observation table

phases.teacher: Pluck a rubber band gently and then stop its motion.
phases.pupils: Compare sound while vibrating and while stopped.

phases.teacher: Set a low-volume vibration demonstration and assign listening positions on different sides.
phases.pupils: Observe the vibrating source, then record where the sound can be heard.

phases.teacher: Check one observation of vibration and observations from at least two sides.
phases.pupils: Explain the source of sound and use two observations to describe its spread.

phases.teacher: Ask what to expect once the band stops moving.
phases.pupils: Predict that the sound stops and explain the link.

plans.follow_up: Repeat with a second source to reinforce the vibration link.

plans.label: Lesson 37
plans.title: Recognise reflected sound
plans.objective: Use two examples to explain why an echo is a reflection of sound.
plans.materials: Echo scenario cards, soft sound source, hard and soft surfaces, comparison diagram

phases.teacher: Tell a short scenario about hearing a repeated voice in a large hall.
phases.pupils: Describe the repeated sound as an echo.

phases.teacher: Demonstrate a quiet sound directed at a hard surface and compare with a soft covering. Use recorded examples if needed.
phases.pupils: Trace outgoing and returning sound for a large hall and a cave.

phases.teacher: Check a diagram and an explanation for both examples.
phases.pupils: Independently explain that sound reflects back from a surface in each situation.

phases.teacher: Ask why the echoed sound is heard after the first sound.
phases.pupils: Explain that the reflected sound travels a longer route.

plans.follow_up: Add arrows to distinguish outgoing and reflected sound.

plans.label: Lesson 38
plans.title: Compare useful and harmful sounds
plans.objective: Sort familiar sounds by their effects and explain why one sound may be useful in one context.
plans.materials: Pictures of alarms, music and traffic; context cards

phases.teacher: Show a school bell card and ask when it helps.
phases.pupils: Name a time a bell is useful.

phases.teacher: Present familiar sound cards and vary their purpose, timing and level using scenario descriptions.
phases.pupils: Sort the sounds and discuss how one changes from helpful to disruptive across situations.

phases.teacher: Check individual classifications and one explanation based on context.
phases.pupils: Submit two useful and two harmful or disruptive examples and explain a context change.

phases.teacher: Ask when recorded music may disturb a lesson.
phases.pupils: Explain using the task and sound level.

plans.follow_up: Use a second context to check reasoning on a borderline example.

plans.label: Lesson 39
plans.title: Reduce noise pollution
plans.objective: Propose a change for a noisy setting and explain how the change would help.
plans.materials: Classroom noise scenario, cloth pads, chair model, planning slip

phases.teacher: Describe chair noise while a class is reading quietly.
phases.pupils: Identify the noise source and whose activity it affects.

phases.teacher: Compare a chair scraping on a surface with the sound when pads are added. Discuss distance and barriers as other options.
phases.pupils: Record the observation, choose one change for a named setting and explain how it reduces noise.

phases.teacher: Check a source-specific proposal supported by an observation or explanation.
phases.pupils: Independently submit one action and describe its effect on that setting.

phases.teacher: Ask which solution acts closest to the source.
phases.pupils: Identify a source-level change and say why it helps.

plans.follow_up: Revisit proposals that only restate that the classroom should be quieter.

plans.label: Review 06
plans.title: Sound Review
plans.objective: Explain an echo and propose a change to reduce sound pollution in a familiar setting.
plans.materials: Echo diagram, noise scenario slips, arrows

phases.teacher: Ask for an example of an echo.
phases.pupils: Name a setting with a suitable reflecting surface.

phases.teacher: Provide a sound path diagram and a second scenario about library noise.
phases.pupils: Add arrows for the reflected sound and suggest a practical noise reduction measure.

phases.teacher: Check both the returning path and the explanation of the measure.
phases.pupils: Submit an echo explanation and a noise solution independently.

phases.teacher: Ask why a soft covering can change a sound in a room.
phases.pupils: Explain that it reduces reflection or absorbs some sound.

plans.follow_up: Review the chosen measure using a familiar noise source.

plans.label: Lesson 40
plans.title: Identify sources of energy
plans.objective: Explain energy in terms of doing work and match four devices or organisms to an energy source.
plans.materials: Pictures of a solar lamp, hydroelectric turbine, windmill and cooking stove

phases.teacher: Show a solar lamp and ask what enables it to work.
phases.pupils: Identify sunlight as a source.

phases.teacher: Connect the ability to do work with a moving or operating device. Compare several textbook energy-source pictures.
phases.pupils: Match four pictured devices to sources and explain one pairing.

phases.teacher: Check four individual matches and a simple definition of energy.
phases.pupils: Submit the four matches and explain energy as the ability to do work.

phases.teacher: Show an unfamiliar wind-powered water pump.
phases.pupils: Name the source and the work done.

plans.follow_up: Explain the difference between a source and a device using another picture.

plans.label: Lesson 41
plans.title: Recognise forms of energy
plans.objective: Identify two forms of energy present in a working device and give evidence for each.
plans.materials: Low-voltage torch, working fan video, energy form cards

phases.teacher: Switch on a torch and point to the illuminated screen.
phases.pupils: Identify light as an observable output.

phases.teacher: Compare light and electrical energy in the torch, then observe movement and sound in a working fan.
phases.pupils: Match forms of energy to observations or device features.

phases.teacher: Check two correctly named forms and specific evidence for each.
phases.pupils: Independently label two energy forms in a device and state the two clues.

phases.teacher: Ask what evidence shows kinetic energy in the fan.
phases.pupils: Point to rotating blades and link the motion to kinetic energy.

plans.follow_up: Use an annotated device picture to reinforce the difference between form and source.

plans.label: Lesson 42
plans.title: Trace an energy transformation
plans.objective: Represent energy changes in two devices with arrows from input to output.
plans.materials: Battery torch, hand-crank fan model or video, arrow strips

phases.teacher: Ask where energy comes from when a torch is switched on.
phases.pupils: Identify the battery as the starting point.

phases.teacher: Model chemical to electrical to light and heat in a battery torch. Show a hand-driven device as a contrast.
phases.pupils: Build arrow chains for both examples and explain the labels.

phases.teacher: Check that input and output forms are in the correct order for two devices.
phases.pupils: Draw and label both transformations independently.

phases.teacher: Ask why an arrow is needed between the energy forms.
phases.pupils: Explain that the arrow represents a change from one form to another.

plans.follow_up: Reconstruct a mixed-up transformation sequence.

plans.label: Lesson 43
plans.title: Explain conservation through transformations
plans.objective: Annotate a transformation diagram to account for useful output and heat or sound.
plans.materials: Illustrations of lamp and fan, energy arrow cards

phases.teacher: Show a picture of a lit lamp that is also warm.
phases.pupils: Identify the light and heat outputs.

phases.teacher: Trace electrical energy into light and heat, then show the fan turning with accompanying sound.
phases.pupils: Annotate useful and other outputs. Explain that energy is transferred or changes form.

phases.teacher: Check a diagram that accounts for useful output and heat or sound.
phases.pupils: Submit one complete transformation and explain where the energy goes.

phases.teacher: Ask what happens to output energy that is not useful for the task.
phases.pupils: Identify an output such as heat transferred to the surroundings.

plans.follow_up: Avoid language that suggests energy disappears when a device runs.

plans.label: Lesson 44
plans.title: Compare renewable and non-renewable sources
plans.objective: Sort examples and explain how replenishment distinguishes the two groups.
plans.materials: Cards for sunlight, wind, flowing water, coal, oil and gas

phases.teacher: Show pictures of a wind turbine and a coal mine.
phases.pupils: Name the energy source associated with each.

phases.teacher: Model how a source can be replenished on a useful timescale. Provide six classification cards.
phases.pupils: Sort the cards by replenishment and defend one example from each group.

phases.teacher: Check classifications and both explanations of replenishment.
phases.pupils: Submit a two-column sort with one reason per group.

phases.teacher: Ask whether coal can be replaced as quickly as it is used.
phases.pupils: Explain that it takes much longer to form.

plans.follow_up: Practise using replenishment as the classification rule.

plans.label: Lesson 45
plans.title: Use energy wisely
plans.objective: Choose two actions that reduce wasted energy and explain how each works.
plans.materials: Illustrated school energy-use scenarios, planning slips

phases.teacher: Show classroom lights on in an empty room.
phases.pupils: Identify the energy use and suggest one response.

phases.teacher: Compare scenarios involving unnecessary lighting, cooling and electronic devices. Discuss actions that preserve the needed service.
phases.pupils: Choose two practical changes and explain which demand each change reduces.

phases.teacher: Check two actions and a specific reason for each.
phases.pupils: Write two actions that reduce wasted energy and explain how they help.

phases.teacher: Ask when switching off a light is appropriate.
phases.pupils: Use room occupancy or daylight as the deciding evidence.

plans.follow_up: Refine proposals that omit how the action saves energy.

plans.label: Review 07
plans.title: Energy Review
plans.objective: Classify sources of energy and label the energy changes in a familiar device.
plans.materials: Energy source cards, fan and torch pictures, arrow strips

phases.teacher: Show a wind turbine and ask how its source is replenished.
phases.pupils: Explain why wind can be treated as renewable.

phases.teacher: Set a source-sort task and a separate device transformation task.
phases.pupils: Classify examples, then label the input and outputs of one device.

phases.teacher: Check both categories and arrows with names of the energy forms.
phases.pupils: Submit the sort and the labelled transformation independently.

phases.teacher: Ask which output helps the device do its intended job.
phases.pupils: Name the useful output from the selected example.

plans.follow_up: Use one further device to distinguish input from output.

plans.label: Lesson 46
plans.title: Trace materials to their sources
plans.objective: Classify objects by their plant, animal, rock, soil or petroleum source and explain one source–material–object link.
plans.materials: Picture cards for wooden chair, wool sweater, metal nail, glass bottle and plastic bottle; transfer cards for cotton shirt, leather shoes, metal coin, mirror and synthetic raincoat; five basic-source labels and source–material–object arrows. Use pictures, not loose glass or sharp nails.

phases.teacher: Show picture cards of a wooden chair, wool sweater, metal nail, glass bottle and plastic bottle. Ask pupils to name each material before identifying its source.
phases.pupils: Name the material shown and predict one possible basic source.

phases.teacher: Introduce the five basic sources. Model textbook examples: plants → wood → wooden chair; animals → wool → sweater; rocks → metal → nail; soil → sand → glass bottle; petroleum → plastic → plastic bottle. Explain the difference between source, material and object.
phases.pupils: Sort picture cards under all five source labels, then arrange each source–material–object chain. Explain the soil–sand–glass example using the textbook chart.

phases.teacher: Use a fresh set of picture cards: cotton shirt, leather shoes, metal coin, mirror and synthetic raincoat. Check all five classifications and one written source–material–object explanation.
phases.pupils: Independently label the basic source for each new object, then write one complete chain, for example petroleum → synthetic cloth → raincoat.

phases.teacher: Ask pupils to identify the source, material and object in the glass-bottle example, then compare it with the plastic-bottle example.
phases.pupils: State soil → sand → glass bottle and petroleum → plastic → plastic bottle, distinguishing each source from its material and object.

plans.follow_up: For pupils who confuse source and material, revisit soil → sand → mirror, then ask them to complete petroleum → synthetic cloth → raincoat.

plans.label: Lesson 47
plans.title: Test absorbency and flotation
plans.objective: Record the response of four materials to equal quantities of water and use the results to order them.
plans.materials: Paper towel, foil, sponge, plastic lid, water drops, basin, table

phases.teacher: Show a sponge and plastic lid and ask what might happen after the same water drop.
phases.pupils: Predict an outcome for each without using the float test as the reason.

phases.teacher: Test equal drops and a fixed wait time for absorbency, then test whether dry samples float in separate trials.
phases.pupils: Record both results for each material in separate columns.

phases.teacher: Check individual records of four samples and a ranking based on one property.
phases.pupils: Rank samples by observed absorbency and state each float result separately.

phases.teacher: Ask if a floating object must absorb water.
phases.pupils: Use two observations from the tests to answer.

plans.follow_up: Recheck the distinction between floating and absorbing.

plans.label: Lesson 48
plans.title: Compare conductivity and light transmission
plans.objective: Use a low-voltage circuit and a light source to compare materials and record the results separately.
plans.materials: School low-voltage battery circuit with test gap, LED, metal and plastic samples, torch and screen

phases.teacher: Show a closed circuit and ask what happens if the test gap is opened.
phases.pupils: Predict what happens to the indicator.

phases.teacher: Model inserting a sample in a teacher-prepared battery circuit. Compare light transmission separately using the same torch and screen.
phases.pupils: Record electrical and light-transmission observations in different columns.

phases.teacher: Check whether each pupil labels the properties and gives one comparison supported by both tests.
phases.pupils: Submit an individual table and explain one result from each test.

phases.teacher: Ask whether letting light through means conducting electricity.
phases.pupils: Use the results to separate the two properties.

plans.follow_up: Revisit the purpose and evidence of each test.

plans.label: Lesson 49
plans.title: Compare heat conduction and elasticity
plans.objective: Compare teacher-prepared heat-conduction observations and test how two materials recover after stretching.
plans.materials: Teacher-prepared heat comparison results, two elastic classroom materials, ruler

phases.teacher: Show a pair of teacher-recorded heat-test measurements and ask which changed first.
phases.pupils: Name one observable difference used for comparison.

phases.teacher: Interpret teacher-prepared results for materials exposed to the same warming conditions. Compare recovery of two materials after a gentle stretch.
phases.pupils: Record which sample transfers heat faster and compare each sample's length before, during and after stretching.

phases.teacher: Check a conclusion for each property with supporting observations.
phases.pupils: Individually name the better heat conductor and the material that recovered more completely.

phases.teacher: Ask what shows elasticity after the force is removed.
phases.pupils: Use the final length relative to the original length.

plans.follow_up: Provide new data to reinforce that heat conduction and elasticity describe different properties.

plans.label: Lesson 50
plans.title: Design an object for a purpose
plans.objective: Build a simple object, test it against one criterion and justify the material choice using measured properties.
plans.materials: Paper, card, plastic sheet, tape, measured water drops

phases.teacher: Show a model container that must protect a paper insert from a splash.
phases.pupils: Name a relevant material property.

phases.teacher: Set a criterion that the insert stays dry after an equal measured splash. Guide pupils to select and assemble a cover.
phases.pupils: Make a small model, perform the agreed test and record whether the insert stayed dry.

phases.teacher: Check a test result and a material choice justified by prior property observations.
phases.pupils: Individually draw the result and defend one material choice using the test evidence.

phases.teacher: Ask which change could be tested fairly next.
phases.pupils: Suggest one change and one fixed condition.

plans.follow_up: Revise the proposal when the material choice lacks measured evidence.

plans.label: Review 08
plans.title: Materials Review
plans.objective: Select a material for a specified purpose and support the choice with two observations.
plans.materials: Property results chart, cards for a bag, a curtain and a handle

phases.teacher: Show a handle card and ask which property would matter.
phases.pupils: Suggest a property relevant to the handle.

phases.teacher: Assign one purpose and give a chart with two sources of evidence about each candidate material.
phases.pupils: Compare choices and connect two observations to the stated use.

phases.teacher: Check an individual recommendation supported by two results.
phases.pupils: Write a material choice and two pieces of evidence.

phases.teacher: Ask how the choice might change for a transparent cover.
phases.pupils: Name a relevant property and identify suitable evidence.

plans.follow_up: Revisit any justification based only on appearance.

plans.label: Lesson 51
plans.title: Explain the effect of gravity
plans.objective: Sketch falling and stationary objects and explain why both are subject to Earth's gravity.
plans.materials: Soft foam ball, paper sketch slips, picture of an object resting on a table

phases.teacher: Release a foam ball and ask what is observed.
phases.pupils: Describe its downward movement.

phases.teacher: Compare the falling ball and the same ball at rest on a table. Explain that gravity acts in both cases and that the table supports the resting ball.
phases.pupils: Draw both situations and show the downward pull of gravity.

phases.teacher: Check two drawings and a statement explaining the supported object.
phases.pupils: Individually label gravity for both examples and explain why the resting object does not fall through the table.

phases.teacher: Ask whether the ball has to move to be affected by gravity.
phases.pupils: Use the resting example as evidence for the explanation.

plans.follow_up: Use a familiar supported object to practise applying the same reasoning.

plans.label: Lesson 52
plans.title: Model Earth's rotation and revolution
plans.objective: Demonstrate both movements with a globe and state their directions and durations.
plans.materials: Globe, marked axis, lamp or labelled Sun model

phases.teacher: Ask what can move when the globe spins in place.
phases.pupils: Describe the globe turning about its axis.

phases.teacher: Demonstrate west-to-east rotation and revolution around the model Sun. Use the view above the North Pole to show direction and compare typical durations.
phases.pupils: Model the two movements and label about one day for rotation and about one year for revolution.

phases.teacher: Check the movement, direction and duration of each on an individual diagram.
phases.pupils: Draw and label one rotation and one revolution independently.

phases.teacher: Ask which movement returns a place to facing the Sun the next day.
phases.pupils: Identify rotation.

plans.follow_up: Repeat the model from the same viewing direction to avoid reversing arrows.

plans.label: Lesson 53
plans.title: Explain day, night and shadows
plans.objective: Use a globe and lamp to explain day and night, then link shadow direction or length to observed changes.
plans.materials: Globe with a marked location, lamp, shadow photo sequence

phases.teacher: Light one side of the globe and ask what the marked place experiences.
phases.pupils: Identify day or night from the light reaching the mark.

phases.teacher: Rotate the globe under the fixed lamp. Compare shadow photos for different times using a fixed marker.
phases.pupils: Identify when the mark enters or leaves the illuminated side and explain one shadow change.

phases.teacher: Check a labelled day/night diagram and an explanation of a change in shadow direction or length.
phases.pupils: Submit the diagram and explain a shadow change using the Sun's apparent position.

phases.teacher: Ask whether the lamp or globe was moved for day and night.
phases.pupils: Identify the globe and explain the model.

plans.follow_up: Revisit the link between Earth's rotation and the apparent movement of the Sun.

plans.label: Lesson 54
plans.title: Present evidence of Earth's motions
plans.objective: Use a labelled model or diagram to communicate one observation of each motion.
plans.materials: Globe, lamp or Sun marker, poster paper and arrows

phases.teacher: Give two sketches of Earth's motion and ask which is about an axis.
phases.pupils: Identify the rotation sketch.

phases.teacher: Ask teams to prepare distinct arrows and model observations for rotation and revolution.
phases.pupils: Display both motions on a labelled model or diagram and explain one observation for each.

phases.teacher: Check one accurate observation from each model and whether the motion labels and arrows agree.
phases.pupils: Individually annotate two sketches and write one observation for each.

phases.teacher: Ask which movement the orbit arrow represents.
phases.pupils: Name revolution and distinguish it from spinning.

plans.follow_up: Provide one motion sketch for pupils who still mix the two.

plans.label: Review 09
plans.title: Earth Review
plans.objective: Explain day and night using a globe and identify the role of gravity in a separate example.
plans.materials: Marked globe, lamp, gravity picture and review slips

phases.teacher: Show a marked location on the illuminated side.
phases.pupils: Identify what the marked place experiences.

phases.teacher: Assign two tasks: model day and night and explain one gravity scenario involving a falling or supported object.
phases.pupils: Demonstrate the rotation and annotate an arrow for gravity on the diagram.

phases.teacher: Check the rotation explanation and why gravity acts in the second example.
phases.pupils: Independently submit the two labelled diagrams.

phases.teacher: Ask why Earth's motion and gravity are different explanations.
phases.pupils: Link each explanation to its own observation.

plans.follow_up: Reteach the example that lacked a clear causal explanation.

plans.label: Lesson 55
plans.title: Identify the parts of a lever
plans.objective: Label effort, load and fulcrum on two everyday examples and explain where effort is applied.
plans.materials: Toy seesaw, diagram of a bottle opener, effort/load/fulcrum labels

phases.teacher: Show a seesaw and ask which part stays at the pivot.
phases.pupils: Identify the support beneath the board.

phases.teacher: Model labelling the pivot, object being moved and point where effort acts. Compare a second lever diagram.
phases.pupils: Mark load, fulcrum and effort on both examples.

phases.teacher: Check all labels and the direction or location of effort.
phases.pupils: Individually label two lever diagrams and explain where the effort is applied.

phases.teacher: Ask pupils to point to the part that turns about the fulcrum.
phases.pupils: Trace the movement of the lever arm.

plans.follow_up: Repeat labelling on an unfamiliar lever picture.

plans.label: Lesson 56
plans.title: Investigate a lever
plans.objective: Compare the effort needed for two load positions and explain the change using recorded observations.
plans.materials: Ruler lever, secured pivot, small load, capped spring scale, results slips

phases.teacher: Show one load position near the pivot and one farther away.
phases.pupils: Predict which will require more effort when the effort point is fixed.

phases.teacher: Keep the pivot, load mass and effort point fixed while changing the load position. Measure the effort for both positions with a spring scale.
phases.pupils: Record both readings and compare the effect of the load distance.

phases.teacher: Check two readings with units and a conclusion supported by the comparison.
phases.pupils: Individually state which position needed less effort and cite the observations.

phases.teacher: Ask why the load mass was kept constant.
phases.pupils: Explain that the test aims to compare position.

plans.follow_up: Use a labelled diagram when pupils confuse load distance and effort distance.

plans.label: Lesson 57
plans.title: Recognise the seven simple machines
plans.objective: Identify examples of simple machines and explain the use of three of them.
plans.materials: Pictures or samples of seven simple machines, labels and matching cards

phases.teacher: Show a ramp and a toy wheel and ask how each helps.
phases.pupils: Suggest what each changes about a task.

phases.teacher: Model identifying the lever, wedge, screw, pulley, inclined plane, wheel and axle, and gear using examples.
phases.pupils: Classify seven examples and explain three functions to a partner.

phases.teacher: Check the seven matches and uses of three distinct machines.
phases.pupils: Independently match the examples and describe how three make a task easier.

phases.teacher: Ask how a wheel with teeth differs from a smooth wheel in use.
phases.pupils: Identify the gear and describe how it can transfer movement.

plans.follow_up: Compare examples for the categories most often confused.

plans.label: Lesson 58
plans.title: Combine simple machines to solve a problem
plans.objective: Build or model a way to move a load using at least two simple machines and show how each helps.
plans.materials: Toy load, ramp, model cart, ruler, tape and planning slip

phases.teacher: Show a small box and a low platform.
phases.pupils: Suggest a safe way to move the box up.

phases.teacher: Set the challenge of using two simple machines. Guide groups to test a ramp with a wheeled cart and record the result.
phases.pupils: Build or sketch the arrangement, move the model load and identify how the incline and wheels help.

phases.teacher: Check that two simple machines are named and that each contribution is independently explained.
phases.pupils: Submit a labelled model sketch and explain the roles of the ramp and wheel and axle.

phases.teacher: Ask what evidence shows each machine helped.
phases.pupils: Cite the raised path and the rolling movement observed.

plans.follow_up: Improve the model by changing one feature and testing the result.

plans.label: Lesson 59
plans.title: Explain a complex machine
plans.objective: Identify at least two simple machines in a complex machine and show how they work together.
plans.materials: Hand egg-beater photo or classroom demonstration, gear and axle labels, arrows

phases.teacher: Show a hand egg beater and ask how turning its handle moves the whisk.
phases.pupils: Point to the input handle and output whisk.

phases.teacher: Trace rotation from the handle and its axle through meshing gears to the whisks. Ask groups to annotate the components they can see.
phases.pupils: Identify the wheel and axle and gears and show how rotation passes between them.

phases.teacher: Check two labelled mechanisms and a clear linked description of the movement.
phases.pupils: Individually annotate the mechanism and explain how both simple machines work together.

phases.teacher: Ask what happens if the gears do not mesh.
phases.pupils: Explain why the input cannot transfer rotation to the whisk as intended.

plans.follow_up: Recheck the path of movement using arrows from the handle to the output.

plans.label: Review 10
plans.title: Machines Review
plans.objective: Compare two lever setups and identify the simple machines in an everyday device.
plans.materials: Two lever sketches with identical loads, everyday-device diagram, review slip

phases.teacher: Show two lever setups and ask which positions differ.
phases.pupils: Compare load position and name what is kept fixed.

phases.teacher: Assign a lever comparison and a device-identification task using labelled drawings.
phases.pupils: Predict which setup needs less effort and identify two simple machines in the device.

phases.teacher: Check an individual effort prediction with a reason and the correctly named mechanisms.
phases.pupils: Submit one lever comparison and label two mechanisms in the device.

phases.teacher: Ask why knowing the pivot position matters.
phases.pupils: Explain that it determines the distances used in the comparison.

plans.follow_up: Practise the question for which the exit slip lacked a reason.
